extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato, classics and philosophy scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Plato's criteria for education, censorship, the arts, music, and civic organisation as discussed in commentary on Book II–III of the Republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of nursery tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Children ought not to learn what they will have to unlearn when they grow up; we must therefore have a censorship of nursery tales, banishing some and keeping others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban stories that are immoral or false as early instruction (examples given: many tales of Homer and Hesiod such as Uranus and Saturn, Zeus inciting Pandarus, Hephaestus binding his mother). Legislators lay down principles for what books are to be written; they do not themselves write them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of the gods: author of good only
rubrics_metrics.description: God must be represented as he is; not as the author of all things, but of good only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid poets saying God is steward of good and evil, that gods cause men to sin, or that God causes sufferings (examples: Athene and Zeus inciting Pandarus, God causing Trojan War, Niobe's sufferings). Such portrayals are 'wicked, suicidal fiction' and must not be uttered by young or old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of the gods: immutable and truthful
rubrics_metrics.description: With God is no variableness or change of form. God is true; he changes not, he deceives not, by day or night, by word or sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject poetical portrayals of gods taking disguises or being changeable; deny stories of gods begging in priestess likeness or prowling in strange disguises. The gods should not be represented as given to lies or deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: lie in the soul vs lie in words
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'lie in the soul' is the corruption of the highest truth and far worse than a mere verbal falsehood; the lie in words is a lesser accommodation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lie in the soul (e.g., representing God as false or immoral) is intolerable. Falsehood in words may be allowed as a 'medicine' for men in certain cases, but its use should be strictly limited—reserved to rulers and employed only for great moral ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purify religion to banish fear
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another motive in purifying religion, which is to banish fear; for no man can be courageous who is afraid of death, or who believes the tales which are repeated by the poets concerning the world below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expunge terrifying afterlife passages (examples: horrors of Cocytus and Styx, squalid mansions of the dead). Such tales are not proper for soldiers; soldiers must be trained not to fear death. Remove lamentations and depictions that encourage fear or cowardice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a high virtue; controlled use of falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth should have a high place among the virtues, for falsehood is useless to the gods, and only useful to men as a medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsehood's employment must remain a privilege of state; common people must not lie to rulers any more than a patient to his physician. The intention and moral effect of any fiction must be considered—'falsely true' speech is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and self-control in youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Our youth must be temperate, and temperance consists in self-control and obedience to authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject poetry and passages that praise drunkenness, gluttony, excessive laughter, amorous excesses, or fear of starvation. Avoid narratives that model bribery, greed, meanness, cruelty, or profligacy (examples: passages praising gifts persuading gods, Achilles' meanness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving guardians imitative/dramatic roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians will have enough to do without imitating. If they imitate they should imitate not meanness or baseness but the good only; the mask which the actor wears is apt to become his face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer descriptive style over imitation for guardians. Do not allow guardians to play inferior parts (women in labour, slaves, bullies, cowards, animals, etc.). Avoid training guardians as actors/rhapsodists who imitate many roles—human nature is 'coined into very small pieces' and one man should play one part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry style: preference for descriptive over imitative
rubrics_metrics.description: All poetry is a narrative of events past, present, or to come; narrative is of three kinds: the simple, the imitative, and a composition of the two. The State prefers the descriptive style with as little imitation as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject polyphonous, pantomimic, or highly imitative compositions that attract youth and corrupt taste. Admit the 'rough, honest poet' rather than complex rhapsodists. Style must conform to subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music: simplicity; allowed and banned modes
rubrics_metrics.description: As our citizens are to be temperate, we may banish mixed Lydian harmonies and convivial Ionian; two remain—the Dorian (for war) and the Phrygian (for peace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject variety of harmony and many-stringed complex instruments (in particular ban the flute). Permit the lyre and the harp in town and the Pan's-pipe in the fields. Harmony should be simple and suitable to the soul's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre: simplicity and congruence with style
rubrics_metrics.description: The style is to conform to the subject and the metre to the style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, suitable metres; the tetrachord and three ratios of metre (3/2, 2/2, 2/1) each have characteristics. Damon the musician is invoked for technical arrangement, but the guiding principle is that metre reflect the simplicity and harmony of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture and painting: conform to simplicity and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture and painting equally with music must conform to the law of simplicity. He who violates it cannot be allowed to work in our city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expose guardians to images of deformity that will 'poison and corrupt their souls'; the city must cultivate a land of health and beauty to provide harmonious influences for the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts and literature: avoid meanness and unseemliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Other artists as well as poets should be warned against meanness or unseemliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All arts (poetry, music, sculpture, painting) should reflect simplicity and moral fitness; corrupting or base representations are to be excluded to protect the guardians' formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians' gymnastics and diet: simple, inuring, temperate regimen
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must abstain from strong drink; they require a simpler kind of gymnastic akin to their simple music; diet rule may be found in Homer—feed heroes on roast meat only, give no fish nor boiled meats, and avoid sweet sauces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians should be inured to changes of food and climate; forbid Sicilian cookery, Attic confections, Corinthian courtezans and other luxuries that lead to gluttony, intemperance, doctors and pleaders. The regimen should support wakefulness, martial readiness, and temperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: State formation and division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Society arises out of the wants of man: first food, then house, then coat; these needs and the possibility of exchange draw individuals together and lead to division of labour—husbandman, builder, weaver, cobbler, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A city needs at least four or five citizens; division of labour creates markets, money, retailers, imports/exports; luxury creates demand for arts and specialists and may lead to war. The construction of the State begins with simple community and proceeds to more complex organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid luxury to prevent social ills
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want not only a State but a luxurious State, the fine arts and luxuries will be wanted; to feed these superfluous mouths we shall need a part of our neighbour's land, and this is the origin of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luxury necessitates armies, doctors, pleaders and brings social corruption; prefer simplicity to limit the growth of exploitative professions and political evils. Encourage citizens to order lives so as to reduce dependence on law and medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of inquiry: begin with the State then the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato preserves the genuine character of Greek thought in beginning with the State and in going on to the individual; under the fanciful illustration of the large letters he implies that he will only look for justice in society, and that from the State he will proceed to the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame ideals at the social/institutional level first (the perfect State) and then consider how justice and happiness coincide at the individual level; use the State as the primary pedagogical and analytical unit when defining civic virtues.
